regional_overview: The week's sharpest development is the instantaneous translation of Hungary's political transition into concrete alliance-solidarity action: Zbigniew Ziobro departed Hungary within hours of Magyar's inauguration, demonstrating that 16 years of Orbán-era friction with EU partners has a measurable half-life measured in hours rather than years. Simultaneously, Romania's political and economic crises have compounded into a structural emergency — the no-confidence vote passed 281-4 with PSD coordinating alongside AUR (a first in post-communist Romanian history), the leu hit 5.27 EUR/RON, the BNR drained €2.2B in April defending the float, and S&P issued formal downgrade warnings — all while a caretaker government incapable of new fiscal commitments sits at the helm during coalition formation. Against this backdrop, the region's two operational cohabitation conflicts — Poland's Tusk-Nawrocki divergence on US troop posture and Czech Republic's Pavel-Babiš impasse over NATO Ankara summit representation — have both escalated simultaneously, revealing a structural vulnerability in how EU semi-presidential systems project coherent NATO policy under divided governments. Ukraine's Victory Day week produced the largest single-story source footprint in any analyzed week (47 sources on the ceasefire), but the analytically novel development was Russia's EW capability redirecting Ukrainian drones into Latvian territory and prompting Latvia's defense minister to resign — a new uncontrolled escalation pathway that none of the region's NATO members have yet formally addressed.

regional_highlights.headline: Magyar inaugurated as PM with 140 votes; Ziobro departs Hungary within hours, ending 16 years of Orbán rule's alliance-friction legacy in a single day
key_facts: Péter Magyar elected PM with 140 parliamentary votes on May 9, 2026
Zbigniew Ziobro — sought by Polish justice authorities — departed Hungary within hours of Magyar's inauguration, before the full cabinet was sworn in
200,000-person Kossuth Square celebration; EU flag returned to parliament façade as deliberate symbolic reversal of 2014 removal

Görög Márta — cross-party legal academic — named justice minister, replacing the nepotism-tainted Melléthei-Barna appointment
First announced foreign visit is Poland; May 25 EU formal agreement remains the primary pending structural milestone
Energy constraints (93% Russian crude, 85% Russian gas, Rosatom nuclear fuel) entirely unaddressed in transition week
regional_highlights.tension: Magyar has a large legitimacy reserve (200,000-person inauguration, 140-vote parliament) but faces embedded institutional constraints — Polt silent, Constitutional Court untouched, KESMA and SPO unaddressed — that the 'years not months' timeline correctly describes; the May 31 ultimatum is a credibility test with no compliance mechanism yet visible

Leu reached intraweek peak of 5.27 EUR/RON, settling at 5.2364; BNR drained €2.2B in April defending the float (reserves now €64.8B)

PNL voted 50-4 against new PSD coalition; AUR declared it will govern only under its own PM; no obvious majority formation path exists

regional_highlights.tension: The compound crisis is self-reinforcing: political uncertainty accelerates currency pressure, currency pressure makes fiscal consolidation harder, fiscal deterioration strengthens the AUR narrative that justifies the very coalition configuration that caused the crisis

Ukrainian drones redirected by Russian EW struck Latvian oil storage; Sybiha apologized to Baltic states and Finland; Latvia's Defense Minister resigned

Hungary returned Oschadbank assets ($40M, €35M, 9kg gold); Zelensky congratulated Magyar
regional_highlights.tension: The Latvia drone incident creates acute friction specifically with Ukraine's strongest European supporters (Baltic states) at the most diplomatically sensitive moment since the war began, while Russia's 4-regiment anti-drone redeployment confirms the deep strike campaign is working — the strategic instrument generating the most results is the same one generating the most alliance friction

cross_cutting_dynamics.title: Hungarian transition triggers immediate Polish accountability result: Ziobro departure as alliance-solidarity proof of concept
cross_cutting_dynamics.assessment: Péter Magyar's inauguration on May 9 produced a direct and immediate consequence in Polish domestic politics: Zbigniew Ziobro — sought by Polish justice authorities, sheltered by Orbán's Hungary, protected from EU extradition mechanisms by the prior government's explicit political choice — departed Hungary within hours of the formal transition, before the full Magyar cabinet was sworn in. Poland's Justice Minister simultaneously announced extradition proceedings. The causal chain is direct and documented: Hungary's domestic_regime shift (Magyar's 140-vote election) removed the political protection structure that had made Orbán's Hungary a viable sanctuary, and Ziobro's departure was the immediate operational consequence. The speed of departure — hours, not days or weeks — confirms that Ziobro himself and his legal team understood that the Hungarian protection was tied specifically to the Orbán government's political will, not to any legal defense that would survive a transition. This interaction is bi-directional in its implications: it simultaneously confirms that Magyar's first alliance-solidarity action was practical rather than rhetorical, and it removes a significant irritant from the PL-HU bilateral relationship at the moment when Hungary is reorienting toward European mainstream. The residual complication is that Ziobro is now in the United States on a TV Republika journalist visa, which Poland's Justice Minister has described as requiring extradition proceedings — a multi-year process that gives Ziobro a platform through the entire 2027 Polish electoral cycle. The HU-PL resolution of the Ziobro dimension has thus displaced rather than closed the accountability dynamic.
cross_cutting_dynamics.significance: This is the first concrete, same-day, documented instance of the Hungarian political transition producing a measurable policy change affecting another country in the region. It validates the structural prediction that Orbán-era friction with EU partners had a political rather than structural basis — but the speed of the Ziobro departure also reveals how dependent that friction was on a single actor's political will, which makes the transition's alignment implications more durable than skeptics predicted. For the regional institutional framework, this demonstrates that EU partner-solidarity norms can be operationalized through government transition faster than through any formal legal or diplomatic process. The Polish-Hungarian bilateral channel — anchored by Magyar's first foreign visit selection of Warsaw — is now structurally repositioned as a cooperative rather than adversarial relationship for the first time in the analytical record.
cross_cutting_dynamics.weakest_link: HU alignment_diplomatic at 4: the Ziobro causal attribution rests on France24 (tier 2) and collapses two analytically separable questions — whether Ziobro departed because of the transition, and whether the timing was a deliberate signal versus a precautionary exit by Ziobro's own legal team. The devil's advocate challenge in the HU report flags this explicitly.
cross_cutting_dynamics.evidence_against_linkage: Ziobro's departure may have been self-initiated based on his own legal team's assessment that the transition eliminated his protection, rather than a deliberate first-act solidarity signal from Magyar's government. If Ziobro departed before receiving any formal communication from the incoming government, the interaction is best characterized as a rational actor response to changed circumstances rather than a coordinated HU-PL alliance action. Additionally, Magyar's government had not yet operationally controlled the Hungarian immigration and justice apparatus at the moment of departure — the full cabinet oath is May 12 — so the 'alliance solidarity' framing may be overattributing intentionality to what was structurally a protection-collapse.
cross_cutting_dynamics.linkage_justification: The temporal sequence is unambiguous (inauguration → departure within hours), the documented causal mechanism is clear (Orbán's political protection was the only barrier to departure, Magyar's election removed it), and both Polish and Hungarian sources confirm the connection. The alternative explanation — Ziobro's self-initiated exit — is compatible with the linkage rather than contradicting it: Ziobro departing because he correctly assessed that Magyar's election ended his protection is still a direct interaction effect from HU domestic_regime on PL domestic_regime.
cross_cutting_dynamics.competing_interpretation: Ziobro's departure was a precautionary self-exit driven by his own legal team's risk calculus, not a deliberate first-act by Magyar's government, and the PL-HU alliance-solidarity framing is being superimposed on what was a rational-actor response to changed political circumstances. Under this interpretation, the interaction is real but its agency is misattributed.

cross_cutting_dynamics.title: Parallel cohabitation conflicts over NATO/defense representation: Poland and Czech Republic simultaneously project incoherent executive voices on alliance questions
cross_cutting_dynamics.assessment: Both Poland and Czech Republic this week exhibit structurally identical cohabitation conflicts in which a president and a prime minister are projecting contradictory signals on NATO and defense questions simultaneously. In Poland: Nawrocki publicly welcomes US troops relocating from Germany to Poland and receives Trump's public attribution of the Poczobut exchange success as 'my friend,' while Tusk urges restraint on the troop relocation and the operational intelligence track (ABW/AW) runs through the government rather than the presidential office. In Czech Republic: Pavel explicitly threatens a constitutional complaint over Babiš's position on NATO Ankara summit representation, a designated resolution meeting fails with Babiš departing through a back entrance, and a June deadline now approaches before the July summit. Both conflicts share a structural origin: EU semi-presidential constitutional systems in which the president retains formal or conventional foreign and defense prerogatives, combined with governing coalitions of opposing political orientation. Both conflicts specifically crystallize around NATO alliance representation questions — who speaks for the country at what level of the NATO architecture. The parallel is structural rather than coordinated: there is no evidence of PL-CZ coordination on cohabitation strategy, no shared institutional mechanism driving the parallel, and the specific disputes are entirely different (basing preferences and intelligence attribution in Poland; summit representation in Czech Republic). The parallel is a structural coincidence produced by the same EU constitutional design under similar political pressure.
cross_cutting_dynamics.significance: NATO's planning and basing decisions depend on member states projecting coherent executive voices. When two of the alliance's most operationally active eastern flank members simultaneously produce divergent executive signals on the same week that the US president publicly chooses a presidential interlocutor over a government interlocutor (Poland), the institutional architecture for NATO eastern flank coherence is under pressure from below. For NATO planning purposes, the Polish case is the more acute risk: Trump's explicit interlocutor preference for Nawrocki — combined with the government holding the operational security relationship — creates a channel mismatch where political signals flow through one executive actor and operational capability flows through another. The Czech case has a harder deadline (June, before July Ankara summit) but a clearer legal resolution mechanism (constitutional complaint).
cross_cutting_dynamics.weakest_link: CZ alignment_diplomatic at 4: the devil's advocate in the CZ report notes that the CGS succession absence check has been miscalibrated for four consecutive weeks, suggesting a possible collection gap in Czech security assessment. The institutional confrontation details are well-sourced (CT24, tier 2; Aktuálně.cz, tier 2) but the substance of the failed Prague Castle meeting is not publicly confirmed beyond the fact of failure.
cross_cutting_dynamics.evidence_against_linkage: These are independent disputes driven by entirely different political contexts. Poland's cohabitation conflict is embedded in a 2027 electoral contest already formally opened by Nawrocki's referendum initiative, with Trump's personal relationship with Nawrocki as the specific catalyst for this week's divergence. Czech Republic's conflict is driven by ANO's weak governing position, SPD's coalition assertiveness, and a specific summit attendance question. The two conflicts share a structural form but have no operational connection — PL and CZ are not coordinating on cohabitation strategy, and the outcomes of each conflict are institutionally independent.
cross_cutting_dynamics.linkage_justification: The linkage is structural rather than causal: both cases are instances of the same design vulnerability in EU semi-presidential systems (presidential foreign policy prerogatives + cohabitation + NATO representation demands), manifesting simultaneously because NATO's 2026 summit cycle is placing specific demands on both countries at the same time. The mechanism is shared constitutional design under shared external pressure, not coordination or contagion. This makes the parallel analytically significant for understanding eastern flank NATO coherence as a systemic, not bilateral, challenge.
cross_cutting_dynamics.competing_interpretation: These are independent domestic political conflicts that happen to involve NATO questions because NATO questions are prominent this week — the ceasefire, the Victory Day cluster, the upcoming Ankara summit. Under this interpretation, any week with high NATO salience would produce visible cohabitation conflicts in semi-presidential EU states, and the parallel reveals nothing specific about Poland-Czech structural alignment.

cross_cutting_dynamics.title: Synchronized central bank hawkish pivots in Poland and Czech Republic both explicitly cite Middle East energy shock
cross_cutting_dynamics.assessment: Both the NBP (Poland) and CNB (Czech Republic) this week shifted their monetary policy signals in the hawkish direction while explicitly attributing the shift to Middle East/Gulf energy price pressures. In Poland, Glapiński stated that the probability of rate hikes has risen explicitly since April, driven by Gulf/Iran energy shock — his framing identifies the external shock as the dominant new variable in the NBP's reaction function. In Czech Republic, the CNB unanimously held at 3.5% but shifted the balance of risks to pro-inflationary, with Middle East risk identified as the dominant factor and a Q2 2026 rate hike explicitly forecast. Both central banks are therefore responding to the same external energy price shock with the same directional policy shift in the same week, without any evidence of coordination between the NBP and CNB. This is a clean coincidence pattern: identical structural condition (Gulf/Iran-driven energy price inflation) independently triggering the same policy response in two closely trade-integrated economies with similar energy import exposure. The parallel has a secondary implication: both fiscal environments are tightening simultaneously, which constrains the governments' room for the defense spending ramps that SAFE (Poland) and Czech creative accounting are both designed to accelerate. Defense spending commitments are being made while monetary conditions tighten — a fiscal-monetary tension that will become more visible if rate hikes materialize in both countries.
cross_cutting_dynamics.significance: The synchronized hawkish pivot quantifies a specific transmission channel from Middle East instability into Central-Eastern European domestic monetary policy. If both central banks follow through with hikes, the two most operationally active NATO eastern flank members (in defense spending terms) will be managing defense budget expansion under tightening monetary conditions simultaneously — compressing the fiscal space that defense financing depends on. Poland's RRF absorption deadline (August 31, 35% absorption rate) and Czech Republic's creative accounting NATO commitment strategy both assume stable-to-loose monetary conditions; a dual rate hike cycle introduces a new constraint into both defense financing architectures.
cross_cutting_dynamics.weakest_link: Both assessments are at 4; the limiting factor is that neither country desk provides the specific energy price data or forward curve that would confirm the transmission mechanism — both cite the Gulf/Iran shock as the stated rationale from central bank communications rather than from independent economic analysis.
cross_cutting_dynamics.evidence_against_linkage: Poland's and Czech Republic's monetary cycles are at different stages and driven by different domestic inflation dynamics. Poland's NBP has held at 3.75% through a different trajectory than the CNB's hold at 3.5%. The fact that both central bank governors cited Middle East risk may reflect a shared rhetorical frame (central banks globally using the same external reference point) rather than a shared transmission mechanism. If domestic inflation in each country is primarily driven by domestic wage growth or services, the external energy reference may be a convenient public framing rather than the operative driver.
cross_cutting_dynamics.linkage_justification: Both Glapiński and the CNB explicitly and independently named the same external shock (Gulf/Iran energy pressure) as the operative new variable in the same week, in economies with similar energy import exposure and similar trade structures. The parallel is mechanistically plausible — both countries import significant energy volumes that are priced by Gulf benchmarks — rather than being purely coincidental. The coincidence explanation (same structural condition, independent responses) is the most parsimonious and the most likely correct, but the shared mechanism makes this analytically significant even as a structural coincidence.
cross_cutting_dynamics.competing_interpretation: Both central banks are responding to globally visible energy market developments that all import-dependent central banks are pricing in this week. The parallel is not specific to CEE — it would appear in any region with energy-importing economies, and selecting Poland and Czech Republic as a pair overfits a global monetary trend to a regional pattern.

cross_cutting_dynamics.title: Romanian AUR governance platform creates a direct forward threat to Ukrainian war financing from within the NATO/EU institutional perimeter
cross_cutting_dynamics.assessment: AUR's published 10-point governance platform explicitly proposes halting all international financial aid — including to Ukraine — until Romania's fiscal deficit reaches 3%. This is not a campaign position but a formal governance platform presented by a party that is now a credible government formation participant following the 281-4 no-confidence vote. The formation arithmetic makes AUR's entry into government a structurally plausible outcome: PNL voted 50-4 against new PSD coalition, AUR declared it will govern only under its own PM, and the 60-day constitutional clock is running. If the window expires toward early elections, current polling suggests AUR would benefit substantially. Ukraine's EU-financed defense budget (UAH 1.56 trillion in the current expansion) is not directly affected by Romanian bilateral policy — the EU loan mechanism operates independently of any single member state's bilateral preferences. However, an AUR-led or AUR-influenced government would represent the first case of a NATO/EU member state in the immediate proximity of the Ukrainian border adopting an explicit policy of conditioning security cooperation on domestic fiscal metrics — a precedent with implications beyond the bilateral channel. The confidence ceiling on this dynamic is capped by RO alignment_diplomatic at 3 and the contingent nature of AUR's entry into government.
cross_cutting_dynamics.significance: Even at speculative confidence, this forward risk is analytically significant because it emerges from within the EU/NATO institutional perimeter — unlike Hungarian Orbán-era friction, which was partially contained by EU legal mechanisms, an AUR-governed Romania that explicitly conditions Ukraine aid on domestic deficit targets would represent a new category of institutional challenge. The precedent-setting dimension matters: if AUR enters government and implements this platform, it establishes that EU member states can formally condition Ukraine support on domestic fiscal conditionality, which other nationalist-populist parties in the region would observe and potentially replicate.
cross_cutting_dynamics.weakest_link: RO alignment_diplomatic at 3: Romania's alignment assessment explicitly notes structural Western orientation and characterizes the AUR platform as a 'forward risk that does not affect current posture.' The dynamic is contingent on a government formation outcome that has not yet occurred and may not occur.
cross_cutting_dynamics.evidence_against_linkage: AUR's governance platform is a negotiating position, not an implemented policy. President Dan has not designated AUR's candidate as PM and has shown no inclination to do so. PNL-USR joint front and Dan's own policy commitments create substantial institutional resistance. Romania's NATO/EU treaty obligations — including all infrastructure commitments and the ECT withdrawal (EU-aligned) promulgated under caretaker powers — are institutionally independent of any government configuration. An AUR-led government implementing the Ukraine aid freeze would also immediately trigger EU conditionality responses that could accelerate Romania's credit downgrade risk, creating a self-deterring mechanism.
cross_cutting_dynamics.linkage_justification: The platform is documented (RO domestic_regime confidence 5, Agerpres tier 2). The causal chain from AUR governance entry to Ukraine aid impact is contingent on multiple intermediate steps (Dan designation, government formation, parliamentary confidence, policy implementation) that have not occurred. The dynamic is included because the analytical record would be incomplete without flagging that one of Ukraine's immediate neighboring NATO/EU states has a credible government formation path in which an explicitly Ukraine-aid-hostile party is a required coalition partner.
cross_cutting_dynamics.competing_interpretation: AUR's platform is a maximalist opening bid in coalition negotiations rather than a governance commitment. If AUR enters government as a junior partner under a PSD prime minister, the Ukraine aid freeze position would be traded away in coalition negotiations against other agenda items, as such positions routinely are in multiparty government formation.

dynamics_considered_and_rejected.candidate_dynamic: EU defense financing parallel: Poland SAFE signing + Ukraine EU loan operationalization as coordinated EU defense buildup
dynamics_considered_and_rejected.reason_rejected: These are institutionally distinct instruments with no operational connection. Poland's SAFE agreement is an EU defense industry financing instrument under a specific legal workaround (existing armed forces fund authority bypassing the presidential veto); Ukraine's EU loan is a bilateral sovereign loan from the EU to a candidate country, operationalized into the national defense budget. The beneficiaries are different (EU member vs candidate country), the legal bases are different, the disbursement mechanisms are different, and the institutions administering each are different. The temporal overlap is coincidental — both processes had long pre-existing timelines independent of the other. Calling this a cross-cutting dynamic would obscure the more significant Poland finding, which is that the SAFE workaround demonstrates government can bypass the presidential veto through existing-law contractual channels — a finding about Polish institutional dynamics, not EU-wide defense financing.

dynamics_considered_and_rejected.candidate_dynamic: Regional far-right positioning: AUR (RO), Mi Hazánk (HU), SPD (CZ) as coordinated nationalist-populist bloc
dynamics_considered_and_rejected.reason_rejected: These three parties are in fundamentally different institutional positions this week that make a coordinated pattern implausible. AUR is actively seeking to form a government (power-seeking phase, just participated in bringing down an incumbent government). Mi Hazánk walked out of the Hungarian inaugural session and submitted immediate constitutional amendments — it is crystallizing as a far-right opposition to Magyar's new government (opposition consolidation phase). SPD in Czech Republic is a coalition partner of the governing ANO, actively using parliamentary machinery to advance its own agenda at ANO's expense (coalition assertiveness phase). No evidence of cross-border coordination between these parties was documented in any of the three country reports. Their actions this week respond to entirely different domestic political logic. The surface similarity (nationalist-populist parties active this week) is a product of reporting selection, not a regional dynamic.

dynamics_considered_and_rejected.candidate_dynamic: Victory Day diplomatic fragmentation: Ukraine, Poland, Czech Republic, Romania all managing the Russia-West symbolic confrontation simultaneously
dynamics_considered_and_rejected.reason_rejected: Victory Day is a calendar event that produces coverage every year. The Ukraine ceasefire collapse, Fico's Moscow attendance, and the various commemorative events across the region are all responses to the same annual symbolic occasion, not a coordinated regional diplomatic development. The Ukraine ceasefire specifically is analyzed in depth in the UA report; the only cross-regional implication (Fico as backchannel, via Slovakia — not in this regional set) is already captured in the UA regional highlight. The other countries' Victory Day coverage (CZ's Vítkov ceremony as 'routine commemorative'; RO and PL reports do not flag Victory Day as significant) confirms there is no cross-cutting pattern beyond the calendar coincidence.

dynamics_considered_and_rejected.candidate_dynamic: Simultaneous ECHR/ECJ compliance defiance: Poland CT president defying ECHR interim order + Hungary Sulyok acknowledging ECJ anti-LGBTQ+ compliance obligation as regional EU rule-of-law divergence
dynamics_considered_and_rejected.reason_rejected: These are movements in opposite directions, not a parallel. Poland's CT president Święczkowski is actively defying an ECHR interim order — escalating institutional non-compliance. Hungary's presidential office is acknowledging EU compliance responsibility on the ECJ anti-LGBTQ+ ruling — signaling a shift toward compliance as part of the Magyar transition. Framing these as a shared dynamic would misrepresent the directional divergence: Poland is moving toward greater ECHR defiance while Hungary is moving toward greater ECJ compliance in the same week. The only commonality is that both countries have active EU rule-of-law files, which is a structural background condition that predates this week and does not constitute a new cross-cutting development.

dynamics_considered_and_rejected.candidate_dynamic: Ukrainian drone Latvia incident triggering visible defensive posture responses from CEE NATO allies (PL, CZ, RO)
dynamics_considered_and_rejected.reason_rejected: No responses appeared. The Latvia drone incident — Russian EW redirecting Ukrainian drones into Latvian territory, prompting Latvia's defense minister's resignation — generated 16 sources in the UA story map but does not appear as a notable development in the PL, CZ, or RO reports this week. The absence is analytically significant (flagged in gaps section) but the absence itself forecloses a cross-cutting dynamic. Constructing one from the Ukraine report alone, without corroborating movement in the other country reports, would violate the apophenia check.

gaps.expected_dynamic: Russian EW redirection of Ukrainian drones into NATO territory (Latvia incident) should produce visible defensive posture signaling from CEE NATO allies, particularly Poland — which borders both Russia (Kaliningrad) and Belarus, and whose ABW report this week explicitly documented Russia's hybrid escalation toolkit.
gaps.observed: The Latvia drone incident — which prompted Latvia's defense minister to resign and generated 16 sources in Ukrainian reporting — does not appear as a flagged development in the PL, CZ, or RO country reports this week. Poland's ABW public report (first in 12 years) documents Russian sabotage network professionalization but does not reference the drone redirection capability specifically. No CEE NATO ally in this regional set made a documented public response to the Latvia incident.
gaps.assessment: The absence could reflect: (1) collection lag — the Latvia incident's implications may not have been fully processed into national security responses by May 10; (2) deliberate restraint — CEE allies avoiding public comment on a NATO internal incident to prevent amplifying Russia's demonstrated EW capability; or (3) a genuine gap in country desk coverage of secondary diplomatic reactions. The strategic significance of the gap is high: if Russia can routinely redirect Ukrainian drones into NATO territory using EW and no CEE NATO ally produces a visible response, the deterrence implications require examination. This is a monitoring priority for next week's cycle — specifically, whether Poland, as the most active NATO eastern flank actor with the most developed hybrid threat awareness, produces any formal or informal response to the Latvia precedent.

gaps.expected_dynamic: Hungary's transition toward European mainstream should produce immediate HU-UA diplomatic normalization signals — particularly given Ukraine's return of Oschadbank assets ($40M, €35M, 9kg gold) and Zelensky's congratulations to Magyar, and given Hungary's prior veto record on EU Ukraine aid packages.
gaps.observed: Magyar's first announced foreign visit is Poland, not Ukraine. No HU-UA bilateral normalization framework or meeting was announced this week. The Oschadbank asset return and Zelensky congratulations are documented but no reciprocal diplomatic commitment from Magyar's incoming government on Ukraine aid or bilateral cooperation is recorded. Hungary's energy constraints (93% Russian crude, 85% Russian gas, Rosatom fuel) remain entirely unaddressed.
gaps.assessment: The Poland-first foreign visit sequence is analytically interpretable as Magyar prioritizing the EU mainstream rehabilitation narrative (highest symbolic value, lowest complexity) before engaging the Ukraine relationship (highest complexity, energy dependency constraints). The absence of an immediate HU-UA normalization signal is consistent with the 'years not months' restoration timeline — but it means that Hungary's most consequential prior obstruction (EU Ukraine aid package vetoes) remains unaddressed through the transition's first week. If no HU-UA bilateral commitment materializes by the May 25 EU formal agreement milestone, the question of whether Magyar's government will continue or modify Hungary's Ukraine aid posture becomes the next gap to investigate.

gaps.expected_dynamic: Romania's government collapse and currency crisis — simultaneous with the formation clock running and S&P downgrade warnings — should produce visible EU-level or IMF-level stabilization signaling, given the RRF August 2026 deadline and the structural precedent of prior Romanian fiscal crises triggering multilateral response frameworks.
gaps.observed: No EU Commission, ECB, or IMF stabilization signal appears in the RO report this week. The interim Finance Minister held emergency calls with Fitch and Moody's (Reuters tier 1) but no multilateral framework engagement is documented. The BNR is managing the currency defense alone (€2.2B April reserve drain). The EU-aligned ECT withdrawal was promulgated under caretaker powers, but no EU-RO emergency fiscal dialogue is recorded.
gaps.assessment: The absence may reflect that the EU's multilateral response threshold has not yet been crossed — S&P warnings rather than an actual downgrade, reserves still at €64.8B despite the drain, and the formation process still within its normal constitutional window. However, if the formation period extends toward the 60-day limit and no government capable of fiscal consolidation is formed, the EU response threshold will be crossed before the NRRP August deadline. The gap in external stabilization signaling should be treated as a leading indicator to monitor: its continued absence in next week's cycle would suggest either EU confidence that formation will succeed, or a collection gap in Romanian external relations coverage.
